steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The lighthouse on Greywater Point had no name, only a number on the maritime charts and a low, constant hum from the old Fresnel lens that turned endlessly above the sea.

Elias had kept it for twenty-seven years.

Every evening, he climbed the spiral stairs as the light sank out of the sky. The metal steps were worn in the center from his boots, a soft shining where others might have called it decay. At the top, he checked the clockwork and the backup battery, wiped the salt film from the glass, and listened to the wind push its shoulder against the windows.

He liked the sound of the lens: a faint grinding, the gentle clack as the mechanism advanced. When fog rolled in, the horn bellowed into the gray and the whole tower thrummed. Alone inside it, Elias sometimes felt as if he were standing in the throat of some vast stone animal calling to its distant kin.

The mainland was four miles of chop and weather away. On clear days, he could see the town like a smudge of color on the horizon: the church steeple, the stacked red roofs. He knew that somewhere in that tangle of streets his younger brother lived with a daughter Elias had never met. Letters came and went twice a month with the supply boat. They were brief, polite things full of small news—fishing quotas, repairs to the pier, a photograph once of a girl standing awkwardly with a violin tucked under her arm. He kept that photograph pinned to a cork board beneath the logbook.

It was the logbook that made the days make sense. Every ship he saw, every shift in the weather, every odd sound in the night—he wrote them down. Storms had their own handwriting in the pages: ink blotched by sudden shakes, lines that ran downhill when a wave hit the rock hard enough to make his pen jump.

One November night, the sea rose up.

The barometer had been falling all afternoon, and the radio spat out warnings with the flat insistence of a metronome: gale, gusts to sixty knots, swells building. Elias made his rounds twice, then three times. He checked the fuel, the backup generator, the emergency lamp that burned with a dull yellow instead of the high white beam.

By midnight, the world outside the glass was nothing but water and blackness, flung in wild arcs. The light swept a pale arm around and around, catching nothing but spray. The horn bellowed and was swallowed whole.

He was brewing coffee on the small iron stove when the radio cracked, not with the usual weather voice but with something raw and panicked.

“—any station, any station, this is the trawler Maribel out of Harren Cove. We’ve lost navigation—repeat, we’ve lost nav and we’re taking on water—coordinates unclear, request guidance—over.”

Elias set the pot down too quickly. It slopped boiling coffee across his hand, but he barely noticed. He crossed the room in two strides, pulled on the headset, and thumbed the transmitter.

“Maribel, this is Greywater Light Station. What’s your last known position?”

Static, and then: “Greywater—thought you were automated—uh, last fix was twelve miles northeast of your point, but the compass is spinning. Can’t see a thing. We just—” The voice broke off with a sharp curse. “We just lost another net. I don’t know which way’s home.”

Elias glanced at the clock, then at the storm charts pinned beside the window. He could not see the boat, but he could imagine where it might be, tossed on the dark, hull shuddering. Somewhere out there, the crew were listening to a stranger’s voice to tell them which way not to die.

“Maribel, listen carefully,” he said, hearing how calm he sounded. “I’m going to bring the main beam ten degrees off its usual sweep. When it lines up dead ahead, you turn to put it on your starboard bow. That should set you south-southwest. Keep her there and you’ll clear the shoals. Do not cut in closer than my tower—those rocks will open you like a tin.”

A pause. Rain hissed against the glass like frying oil.

“Copy that, Greywater. We’re in your hands.”

He climbed to the lantern room, every step counted, every breath a measured thing. The tower shuddered, but the machinery held. He disengaged the automatic rotation and, hand on the cold metal rail, began to turn the lens himself, feeling the weight of it in his shoulders and wrists.

The beam swung like a slow, searching eye across the storm, then steadied where he wanted it. He held it there, muscles locking, the light burning a white tunnel through the chaos.

Time lost its shape. His arms ached. Once, a wave hit the rock so hard that he staggered and the beam jittered; he gritted his teeth and steadied it again. The horn bellowed on.

At last, the radio crackled.

“Greywater, this is Maribel. We’ve got the light on starboard, seaway easing, depth increasing. I—” The man’s voice broke again, this time with something like laughter. “We’re clear. You just walked us out of hell, lighthouse. Drinks on us if you’re ever in town. Maribel out.”

Elias let the lens fall back into its slow clockwork sweep. He eased his hands off the rail and realized they were shaking. Down below, the stove had gone out, the coffee grown a cold skin.

He did not answer the radio; there was no need. He went instead to the logbook and opened it to a fresh page. His pen waited above the paper for a long moment.

“November 13,” he wrote at last. “2230 to 0135. Severe storm, visibility near zero. Assisted trawler Maribel to safe water using manual beam adjustment.”

He hesitated, then added a second line.

“Light performed as required.”

Outside, the gale began to slacken. The great voice of the horn fell silent; the sea’s roar dimmed to a hoarse whisper against the rock. In the east, a seam of gray marked where dawn would come.

Elias climbed once more to the lantern room. The glass was fogged along the bottom edge, and he wiped it clear with the side of his sleeve. The mainland was still not visible, only the broad, breathing dark of the ocean.

He knew that in town, the Maribel would limp into harbor with a story to tell, full of shouting and spray and the sudden appearance of a beam where no human hand was supposed to be. They would raise glasses to Greywater Light and to the keeper they had thought was long gone. Perhaps, he thought, his brother would be there. Perhaps the girl with the violin would hear his name for the first time in years.

The notion surprised him with its warmth.

He stood with his hands in his pockets as the sky paled and shapes emerged from the night: the black teeth of the shoals, the far-huddled line of roofs, the white thread of a road. The light turned on above him, steady and uncomplaining.

“Back to it,” he murmured to the machinery, to the tower, to the sea and to himself.

Greywater Light swept its great beam over the waking world, and the keeper watched, as he always had, to make sure that it never faltered.
